passages.context: Chapter 10 describes the office of the subdeacon assisting a bishop who celebrates solemnly. Paragraph 2 distinguishes caligae from sandalia and directs that the pair be taken from the credence, carried on a basin or veil beneath a second silk covering, and raised in both hands. With one of the bishop's attendants assisting, the subdeacon kneels beneath the cappa and vests the right leg and foot first and then the left. The passage controls the two-object distinction, preparation, carrier, covering, order, and combined wearing formation. It does not prescribe fabric, color, ornament, dimensions, fastening, stocking height, or shoe construction.

passages.context: Section 5 directs the pastoral-staff minister to hold the uncovered staff with the end of his cotta covering his right hand. Section 6 directs the mitre minister to wear from his neck an oblong silk veil or cloth, used to support the mitre so that he does not touch it with bare hands, unless he is vested in a cope. The governing text calls the mitre textile velum or mappa sericea oblonga; it does not use the later conventional headword vimpa in this locus.

passages.context: Paragraphs 1-2 locate the episcopal seat according to sanctuary and choir arrangement. Paragraph 3 prescribes three covered steps, a high and elevated seat made as a cathedra and immovable throne, a silk covering matching the other appointments, and a conditional canopy; it assigns this seat to the bishop's solemn Vespers and Mass. Paragraph 4 gives the episcopal seat to a cardinal present and places the celebrating bishop at the faldstool on the Epistle side.

passages.context: Paragraphs 1–4 distinguish the precious, gold-cloth, and simple mitres by material and ornament and assign their principal uses. The precious mitre is associated with more solemn feasts and normally alternates with the lighter gold-cloth mitre during solemn Vespers and Mass; the gold-cloth mitre is assigned to specified penitential seasons and functions, with stated exceptions; the simple mitre is assigned to Good Friday and Offices and Masses of the Dead. Paragraphs 5–9 delimit a bishop's use of the pastoral staff by place or permission; distinguish long processions, in which a minister bears it immediately before him with both hands and raised from the ground, from short processions, in which the bishop may carry it in his left hand; enumerate uses at pontifical Vespers and Mass; and exclude Offices and Masses for the Dead.
passages.notes: Printed pp. 51–53 were inspected at the rendered page images; OCR was used only for navigation and transcription checking. The passage identifies hanging vittae and some mitre materials and ornament, but does not prescribe a single universal profile, height, construction method, iconographic program, or dimensions. Its Holy Week provision predates the restored Holy Week and must be reconciled with the operative 1955–1962 books before a detailed Good Friday composition is presented. The pastoral-staff provisions establish ceremonial use and handling relationships, not material, dimensions, ornament, exact profile, or a crosier stand; their ordinary provisions remain subject to any competent post-1948 amendment applicable at the 1962 horizon.

passages.context: Numbers 10-19 give the bishop's vesting sequence for Solemn Pontifical Mass. After the initial vesting and Terce, n. 18 directs that the cope be removed and that the bishop be vested first in the tunicle and then in the same manner in the dalmatic; the deacon and subdeacon tighten cords placed on each side over the shoulders. Number 19 then directs that the chasuble be put on after the gloves. The passage therefore controls the identity of the pontifical tunicle and pontifical dalmatic as two distinct, successively layered episcopal vestments beneath the chasuble, and supports shoulder cords on the form described by this ceremonial. It does not establish a universal cut, dimensions, ornament, textile, sleeve relation, or reliable isolated visual distinction from the ministers' garments.
passages.notes: Read at the rendered page images, printed pp. 115-116 (artifact PDF pp. 126-127). This pre-1962 witness remains subject to the later 1962 Missal's rubrics; Rubricae generales n. 134 confirms the layered pontifical use at the edition horizon and permits omission for a reasonable cause.

passages.context: The chapter gives the ceremonial sequence for Solemn Pontifical Mass celebrated by a bishop and cross-references the ministers, vesting, altar preparation, books, vessels, insignia, and handoffs described elsewhere. In paragraph 7, the Epistle subdeacon brings the sandalia and caligae from the credence on a basin, with his hands veiled and the footwear covered by another veil. With two episcopal attendants he removes the ordinary shoes and vests the right foot first and then the left, while six or eight kneeling acolytes raise and spread the hem of the cappa. This controls liturgical occasion, preparation, ministers, order, and the replacement of ordinary footwear. It does not control the objects' material morphology or establish that every bishop-shaped shoe or stocking is pontifical footwear.

passages.context: Chapter 11 governs a Pontifical Mass for the Dead. Paragraphs 1-2 require black vestments but expressly direct that the bishop not use sandals, gloves, or pastoral staff, and that the prayers for the sandals and gloves be omitted. The passage therefore establishes a negative branch: pontifical footwear is not black footwear and is not used merely because a bishop celebrates. It does not establish a general rule for every non-Mass episcopal function or every privileged prelate.
